# Diagnosing Rough Idle and Stall in a 1998 Honda Accord V6

A rough idle that transitions into a stall after roughly ten minutes of operation is a classic symptom of a failing engine management system, often pointing toward thermal instability or a specific sensor failure rather than a mechanical fault. In the case of the 1998 Honda Accord V6, the fact that the vehicle starts fine even after stalling and runs smoothly under load suggests the ignition system and fuel pump are likely functional. The core issue usually lies in how the Engine Control Unit (ECU) manages air-fuel mixture when the throttle plate is nearly closed and engine heat soak occurs.

The diagnostic path begins by analyzing the reported transmission code regarding the "shift control valve." While the user has verified shifting performance, it is critical to understand that on many OBD-II systems from this era, a generic powertrain code might be logged due to a temporary lack of communication between the Transmission Control Module (TCM) and the ECU. If the engine stalls while stopped but restarts immediately, the TCM may log a fault because it expects a certain RPM signal that never arrives. This is likely a secondary symptom rather than the root cause; clearing the code won't fix the stall, but ignoring it might mask a deeper electrical issue.

The most probable culprit for an idle that roughens up after ten minutes of driving is the coolant temperature sensor (CTS) or its wiring harness. As the engine warms up, the ECU expects the CTS to report a specific resistance value corresponding to the coolant temperature. If the sensor develops an internal open circuit or if the wiring degrades with heat, the ECU may suddenly revert to "open loop" mode at idle. In this state, it cuts off fuel injection based on a default logic that assumes a cold engine, causing the RPM to drop below the stall threshold. This explains why the problem manifests after the car has been driven for ten minutes but not immediately upon starting.

Another significant factor is the interaction with the Air Conditioning system. When the A/C is engaged, the compressor engages the accessory belt, adding load to the crankshaft. If the idle air control valve (IACV) is clogged with carbon deposits or if its stepper motor is failing, it cannot increase the idle speed by opening the throttle plate enough to compensate for this extra load combined with a warm engine in open loop mode. The result is an unstable idle that collapses into a stall. Cleaning the throttle body was a correct first step, but the IACV itself may require cleaning or replacement if it fails to hold position under load.

Vacuum leaks are also a primary suspect for rough idles, particularly on older engines where rubber hoses dry rot over time. A small leak can be negligible at high RPMs but becomes catastrophic at idle when the manifold vacuum is highest. However, since the user has already inspected for this, attention must shift to electrical continuity and sensor calibration. Using an OBD-II scanner with live data capability is essential here. You need to monitor the Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) while the car is idling after it has warmed up. If the STFT values are wildly positive (e.g., +15% or higher), the ECU is leaning out due to a vacuum leak or a bad oxygen sensor, forcing the mixture too lean for stable idle.

Finally, consider the ignition switch contacts. Although the user checked the switch, a worn contact inside the switch can cause intermittent power loss to the ECU or fuel pump relay specifically when the key is in the "Run" position and the engine is cold, but this usually presents as a no-start condition. Given the specific timing of the stall after ten minutes, thermal expansion and contraction of electrical connectors are more likely suspects. Check all grounds near the engine bay, especially those connected to the ECU and IACV, ensuring they remain tight and free of corrosion. If the transmission code persists after clearing it and verifying no vacuum leaks exist, focus your troubleshooting on the CTS wiring and the IACV functionality under load conditions.
